/MONDAY NIGHT THROUGH SUNDAY/...
Issued at 224 PM CDT Sun Oct 11 2026

The front finally drops into the region late on Tuesday, but it will 
be slowing its progress as it arrives. Moisture pushing northward 
toward the boundary will lead to the first of a few rounds of 
showers and thunderstorms developing Tuesday night along and behind 
the front. This round will favor northern portions of our forecast 
area as guidance has slowed the progression of the front from prior 
forecasts. Additional pockets of showers and thunderstorms continue 
through the day Wednesday with the front slowly sinking southward. 
Then finally one more focused round is expected Wednesday night into 
Thursday as another more potent trough pushes eastward, briefly 
lifting the front back north again before following it up with an 
even stronger cold front Thursday night into Friday.

Although we couldn't completely rule out any severe weather threat, 
convection looks to be focused along and behind the front, and thus 
elevated in nature. Wind shear is also modest but does increase as 
Thursday's trough moves through. The primary threat, though, will be 
locally heavy rainfall. The moisture feeding into this system is 
quite extreme for this time of year, with precipitable water values 
approaching 2 inches. This will lead to the potential for heavy 
rainfall rates in areas of convection, but the gradual progression 
of the front southward should help to mitigate the threat for these 
heavy rainfall rates to linger too long in one spot. If, however, we 
do see multiple rounds of heavy rainfall, or storms training over 
the same location, then the threat for flash flooding will increase. 
Regarding amounts, ensemble guidance shows high confidence (near 100 
percent) that all areas will receive at least some rainfall in the 
Tuesday night through Thursday time period. Among the LREF, more 
than 50 percent of members produce at least 1 inch of rain across 
most of the area during this time frame, and up to 25 percent 
produce at least 2 inches. A lower probability (10 percent) worst 
case scenario could result in 3+ inches if storms line up and linger 
in one spot.

Thursday night's cold front ushers in a pattern change, shifting us 
toward much cooler and drier conditions. Although guidance agrees on 
the general timing, there remains considerable variance in the 
intensity of the air mass behind this front. This all stems from how 
to handle the interaction between a northern stream trough and the 
trough over the western US. The northern stream trough is still over 
eastern Asia at this time and still needs to round the Aleutian low 
and skirt the western Canadian ridge before arriving in the central 
US Thursday. The western trough has already cut itself off over 
Oregon where it will wobble around over the next several days. The 
disagreement comes with whether to absorb this trough with the 
incoming northern stream wave or to keep some of this energy cut off 
over the Southwest US. That depends both on how the north stream 
wave tracks and also where the cut off low wobbles. These cut off 
lows have been some of the more notoriously unpredictable features 
of modern meteorology. Subtle wobbling of this low further east will 
enable a more complete merging of the two waves, while wobbling 
westward would make that merger more difficult.

Guidance sources which favor a full merging of these waves generate 
a much deeper trough with more cold air behind it aimed directly at 
the central US and our region. Guidance which favors only a partial 
interaction track the northern trough further east, pointing the 
cold air push toward New England leaving more modest cool 
temperatures for our area. In the recent few days, the two camps 
have been largely lining up with the parent model systems, with GEFS 
members bringing a deeper trough and intense local cold air while 
ENS members feature a lower amplitude trough and milder conditions 
locally. With the 12Z run there has been a bit more merging of the 
two camps, with about 25 percent of GEFS members now siding with the 
warmer ENS solution and now 20 percent of ENS solutions favoring the 
colder GEFS solution. The GEPS has been more evenly split, but 
overall favoring the warmer ENS solution. What this all means for us 
locally is a shift toward cooler temperatures is coming! On the 
warmer end, we'll be looking at highs near 70, much cooler than we 
have been but near normal for this time of year. On the colder end, 
we would be seeing highs closer to 50 with lows dropping near 
freezing. The latest probabilistic NBM shows the likelihood of 
freezing temperatures at 10 to 30 percent across the region this 
weekend, though this blended guidance is usually a bit slow to react 
to changes and emerging ensemble consensus.
